paper.title_en: Broadening the Scope of Axion Searches: Reflector Haloscope Experiments for Broadband Axion Detection and Collider Probes of Supersymmetrized Axion Models
paper.abstract_en: <p>Axions are pseudoscalar particles that are a compelling addition to our theories of high-energy physics as they can solve two long-standing problems in modern physics. Firstly, cosmological and astrophysical observations indicate that the vast majority of the matter content of our universe is made of dark matter, a substance which cannot be described by the existing particles of the standard model of particle physics. A second major problem in modern physics is a lack of charge-parity (CP) symmetry violation in the strong force which could only arise from our current models through fine-tuning. The axion was initially proposed as a mechanism to naturally cancel the CP violation in the strong force, but it also proved to be a promising candidate for particle dark matter. Many experiments search for axion dark matter by measuring the conversion of axions into photons in a strong magnetic field. The Broadband Reflector Experiment for Axion Detection (BREAD) is one such experiment which uses a reflective surface to focus a photon signal onto an antenna or sensor. BREAD ultimately aims to search for axion-photon signals at frequencies as high as the infrared regime, but this work will focus on the instrumentation and analysis for a pilot version of BREAD which searched for axion-like particle and dark photon signals in a frequency range of 10.7 &minus;12.5 GHz. We will also discuss efforts to extend sensitivity of BREAD to the mm-wave range by, for example, exploiting a comb of resonant modes between a BREAD reflector and a secondary parabolic reflector. Finally, we discuss modeling of a supersymmetrized axion model and a sensitivity analysis of the ATLAS experiment to this model. While the axion-photon coupling is a relatively generic probe of axion models, there are some models, like the supersymmetric axion model introduced in this thesis, which can evade direct-detection axion-photon searches like BREAD. We will highlight the importance of complementing direct-detection experiments like BREAD with other probes of axion physics such as the collider sensitivity discussed here.</p>
